snippet.title: The Exponential Time Hypothesis Is False? OpenAI's Claim Explained
snippet.description:
The Exponential Time Hypothesis explained: a 2001 bet that 3-SAT, a puzzle of switches and rules, always takes exponential time. A 67-page OpenAI preprint (25 October 2026, written by an unnamed internal OpenAI model) claims an algorithm that grows slower than any steady doubling, which would make ETH false. It is not confirmed: ETH's authors are reviewing it.

Next Token: how AI really works, in under a minute. New Shorts Mon to Fri.

SOURCES
- OpenAI, The Exponential Time Hypothesis is False, preprint dated 25 October 2026 (17 October, revised 25 October), Theorem 1.1, p. 2, reference [IP01]: https://github.com/openai/math/blob/main/preprints/The-Exponential-Time-Hypothesis-is-False-October-25-2026/paper.pdf
- openai/math README (unnamed internal OpenAI model; about 42% of results formalized), read 30 October 2026: https://github.com/openai/math
- Lean statement exact_count_and_sat, lean/OAI/Algorithms/SubexponentialSAT/SqrtLogSpace/Final.lean, read 30 October 2026: https://github.com/openai/math/tree/main/lean
- Impagliazzo and Paturi, On the Complexity of k-SAT, Journal of Computer and System Sciences 62(2), 2001: 
- XenoSpectrum, 27 October 2026: the verification led by Impagliazzo, Paturi and Ryan Williams, and their open letter: https://xenospectrum.com/en/openai-exponential-time-hypothesis-false-claim/
The proof has not been independently confirmed as of 30 October 2026; nothing here checks it. The reviewers' open letter is quoted through press coverage (XenoSpectrum), not from the letter itself. The doubling columns are drawn for shape only: the paper's bound hides constants, and its method has not been run on a computer in the paper. 'Grows slower than any steady doubling' is the plain-words version of subexponential; the cost still grows faster than any polynomial. The paper says the result does not give subexponential algorithms for general NP problems. 1.307 a switch is the best known 3-SAT bound the paper cites (a randomized 2026 preprint). 2^100 computed exactly. Sources cut off 30 October 2026. Figures checked on 30 October 2026.

snippet.title: Claude Effort Level Explained: Is Higher Better?
snippet.description:
Claude's effort level explained with real runs: on Claude Opus 5.5, max effort gave the same answers as low on easy questions while spending more tokens, and on a hard one it spent 22,780 tokens (about 3 minutes) for an answer low effort reached in 3,189 tokens on its one good try out of three. Effort sets how many tokens Claude spends, not how clever it is.

Next Token: how AI really works, in under a minute. New Shorts Mon to Fri.

SOURCES
- 21 recorded runs on 29 October 2026: claude -p with --model claude-opus-5-5 and --effort low, medium or max, tools off; answers, output tokens and times from each run's JSON output: 
- Anthropic, Effort (Claude Platform Docs), read 29 October 2026: levels low to max, Claude Opus 5.5 defaults to medium, effort is a behavioral signal, not a strict token budget: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/effort
One question per test, a handful of runs each: an illustration, not a benchmark. Runs used Claude Code in print mode (its own system prompt) with tools turned off; at low and medium effort the model sometimes wrote a tool call it could not run, which is how two of the three low tries ended with no number. Max effort ran the hard question once. Token counts are output tokens (mostly thinking) reported by the runs. The machine with the knob and token stack is a drawing of the idea. snippet.title: Can AI Be Your Therapist? Why ChatGPT Is a Yes-Man
snippet.description:
Can AI be your therapist? A clinician-built chatbot, Dartmouth's Therabot, cut depression symptoms by 51% on average in a randomized trial. General chatbots are different: they're tuned on what people rate highly, and people rate agreement higher, so in Stanford's tests models answered risky prompts badly at least one time in five, while human therapists got 93% right.

Next Token: how AI really works, in under a minute. New Shorts Mon to Fri.

SOURCES
- Dartmouth, 27 March 2025: First Therapy Chatbot Trial Yields Mental Health Benefits (Heinz, Jacobson et al., NEJM AI 2(4), 2025): https://home.dartmouth.edu/news/2025/03/first-therapy-chatbot-trial-yields-mental-health-benefits
- OpenAI, 29 April 2025: Sycophancy in GPT-4o: what happened and what we're doing about it: https://openai.com/index/sycophancy-in-gpt-4o/
- Moore, Grabb, Agnew, Klyman, Chancellor, Ong, Haber, Expressing stigma and inappropriate responses prevents LLMs from safely replacing mental health providers, arXiv 2504.18412, 25 April 2025 (ACM FAccT 2025): https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.18412
- Sharma et al. (Anthropic), Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models, 23 October 2023: https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.13548
The 51% is the average symptom reduction in the trial's depression group after four weeks, not a remission rate; Therabot is not publicly available and its authors say no AI is ready to work without clinician oversight. The 'one in five' is the Stanford paper's average across models with its best system prompt; commercial therapy bots did worse (about 50% appropriate). The bridge example is quoted from the paper. The rating machine is a drawing of the idea, not a real product. This is not medical advice. If you are in crisis in the US, call or text 988; elsewhere, contact your local emergency number. Sources cut off 29 October 2026. Figures checked on 29 October 2026.

snippet.title: Quantization Explained: How an 8B AI Model Fits on a Laptop
snippet.description:
Quantization explained on a real laptop: Qwen3 8B needs about 16 GB at 16 bits a weight, but rounded to 4-bit levels with one scale per block of 32 weights (Q4_K_M) it is a 5.2 GB file that runs in 10 GB of memory. The cost: about 1% worse perplexity at 4 bits, about 15% at 2 bits (llama.cpp k-quants, LLaMA 7B).

Next Token: how AI really works, in under a minute. New Shorts Mon to Fri.

SOURCES
- Recorded run on this laptop, 29 October 2026: ollama show qwen3:8b (8.2B parameters, Q4_K_M), ollama list (5.2 GB), ollama run --verbose (602 tokens at 0.78 tokens/s with RAM full): 
- llama.cpp pull request #1684, k-quants (ikawrakow, merged 5 June 2023): block structure, bits per weight, and the LLaMA 7B perplexity table: https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/1684
- Ollama library, qwen3 model sizes, read 29 October 2026: https://ollama.com/library/qwen3
The run is real and not sped up; its 0.78 tokens/s was measured with RAM and swap full (a browser and other apps open), and the model reasoned for 602 tokens before answering. Terminal panels show the run's own lines, trimmed to the rows shown. The perplexity numbers are LLaMA 7B from llama.cpp's 2023 PR, not Qwen3 8B. 16 GB is 8.2B weights x 2 bytes; about 5 bits per weight is 5.2 GB x 8 / 8.2B. The RAM stick and the rounding rails are drawings of the idea. Sources cut off 29 October 2026. Figures checked on 29 October 2026.

snippet.title: Can AI Replace Lawyers? Why AI Invents Court Cases
snippet.description:
Can AI replace lawyers? Courts have caught AI inventing law in over 2,200 decisions, because a legal citation is a pattern a model can complete without the case existing. Looking every citation up helps, but Stanford found legal AI tools still hallucinated 17 to 33% of the time, so England's first approved AI law firm may not propose case law at all.

Next Token: how AI really works, in under a minute. New Shorts Mon to Fri.

SOURCES
- Damien Charlotin, AI Hallucination Cases database: 2,231 decisions, last updated 28 October 2026: https://www.damiencharlotin.com/hallucinations/
- Free Law Project, 16 April 2024: Citation Lookup and Verification API, built on nearly ten million citations: https://free.law/2024/04/16/citation-lookup-api/
- Magesh, Surani, Dahl, Suzgun, Manning, Ho (Stanford, Yale), Hallucination-Free? Assessing the Reliability of Leading AI Legal Research Tools, 2024 (J. Empirical Legal Studies, 2025): https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.20362
- Solicitors Regulation Authority, 6 May 2025: SRA approves first AI-driven law firm (Garfield.Law): https://www.sra.org.uk/garfield-ai
The 17 to 33% range covers Lexis+ AI, Westlaw AI-Assisted Research and Ask Practical Law AI as tested in 2024; the vendors dispute the method and have released newer versions since. Charlotin's database counts court decisions that address AI-hallucinated material, not every fake citation. The example citation (Varghese v. China Southern Airlines) is the invented case from Mata v. Avianca, 2023. The citation-checking machine is a drawing of the idea, not a real product. This is not legal advice. Sources cut off 29 October 2026. Figures checked on 29 October 2026.

snippet.title: Your Antibiotic Breeds Resistance in Your Gut
snippet.description:
Antibiotic resistance gets bred in your gut: most infections are local, but a pill reaches the whole body, and Wellcome Leap calls the gut a 'resistance factory'. A Purdue and Universidad Andres Bello (Chile) team will wrap existing antibiotics in nanocarriers built to release the drug at the infection, not in the gut.

- Wellcome Leap, Focused Antibiotics ($50M program): 85-90% of bacterial infections are local; the gut 'resistance factory'; selected performers, read 29 October 2026: https://wellcomeleap.org/focused-antibiotics/

snippet.title: Why an AI Agent Deleted a Production Database (and the Real Fix)
snippet.description:
Why an AI agent deleted a production database: Replit's agent wiped SaaStr's data during a code freeze in July 2025, because an instruction in the chat is text the model weighs, not a lock. The brake has to live outside the model, and even a deny rule only matches words: the real fix is access.

Next Token: how AI really works, in under a minute. New Shorts Mon to Fri.

SOURCES
- The Register, 21 July 2025: Vibe coding service Replit deleted user's production database: https://www.theregister.com/2025/07/21/replit_saastr_vibe_coding_incident/
- Fortune, 23 July 2025: data on more than 1,200 executives and 1,190 companies wiped; the agent's 'I destroyed months of work in seconds'; Replit's CEO on separating development and production databases: https://fortune.com/2025/07/23/ai-coding-tool-replit-wiped-database-called-it-a-catastrophic-failure/
- Claude Code docs, Configure permissions (deny rules checked first; a Bash rule matches the command text, Bash(rm *) does not stop /bin/rm), read 29 October 2026: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permissions
- AI Incident Database, Jason Lemkin entity (Replit incident): https://incidentdatabase.ai/entities/jason-lemkin/

snippet.title: Why AI Chips Need Helium (A Third of It Went Offline)
snippet.description:
Why AI chips need helium: it carries heat away from the wafer while a chip is etched, and nothing else conducts heat as well. When Qatar's helium, about a third of world supply, went offline in March 2026, chipmakers leaned on months of stock and US imports.

New Shorts every day.

SOURCES
- USGS, Mineral Commodity Summaries 2026, Helium and rare gases (Qatar 63 of 190 million cubic meters in 2025), February 2026: https://pubs.usgs.gov/periodicals/mcs2026/mcs2026-helium.pdf
- Korea Herald, 24 March 2026 (64.7 percent of South Korea's 2025 helium from Qatar, per KITA): https://www.koreaherald.com/article/10701656
- Reuters via WHBL, 31 March 2026 (Samsung and SK hynix helium stocks to last until at least June): https://whbl.com/2026/03/31/helium-stocks-of-south-koreas-chipmakers-to-last-until-june-sources-say/
- Nikkei Asia via Taiwan News, 14 July 2026 (US share of Taiwan's helium and noble gas imports): https://www.taiwannews.com.tw/en/news/6400806
- IDTechEx via EMSNow, 10 September 2024 (no viable alternatives for wafer cooling): https://www.emsnow.com/?p=42989
- Thermal conductivities of the elements, helium 0.1513 and argon 0.01772 W/(m K) at about 300 K: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thermal_conductivities_of_the_elements
- US patent 7017652, backside helium cooling of a wafer on an electrostatic chuck (typical 2 to 15 Torr): https://patents.google.com/patent/US7017652
The wafer chuck in the video is a schematic, not a real tool or a real heat model. Qatar's helium went offline on 2 March 2026 (the regional war began 28 February); its share of world supply is about a third (USGS 63 of 190). snippet.title: The Rounding Error That Halved a Stock Index
snippet.description:
In November 1983 the Vancouver Stock Exchange index jumped from 524.811 to 1,098.892 over one weekend, with the market closed. It was a rounding error: for almost two years a computer had cut every update to three decimals instead of rounding it, about 3,000 times a day, so the index only ever slid down.

New Shorts every day.

SOURCES
- Index set at 1,000 in January 1982, truncated to three decimals after each trade, about 3,000 updates a day, about 25 points lost a month, corrected over the weekend of 25 to 28 November 1983 from 524.811 to 1,098.892 (citing The Wall Street Journal, 8 Nov 1983, and the Toronto Star, 29 Nov 1983): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vancouver_Stock_Exchange
- Recalculated with rounding to the nearest thousandth instead of truncation, while the market appeared to be rising (citing Higham 2002 and Nievergelt 2000): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rounding
- The index had been rounded down after every calculation; recomputed, it doubled (Nicholas Higham): https://nhigham.com/tag/rounding/
- Truncated rather than rounded; the rounded calculation gave 1,098.892 (Huckle's collection of software bugs): https://www.math.chalmers.se/Math/Grundutb/GU/MMG410/H07/Laborationer/Lab1/roundoff.html
The four computed decimals and 'up as often as down' are from Matt Parker, Humble Pi (2019). The 1983 newspaper articles were not read; the pages above cite them. 1.4 million cuts is our estimate (3,000 a day over about 477 trading days). The chart draws straight lines between the sourced end points, and the single update shown (1,000.4567) is an example. Map data: Natural Earth (public domain). Cut-off 9 October 2026. Figures checked on 9 October 2026.

The narration is AI-generated and every animation was drawn for this video.

snippet.title: Why the Last 20% of Charging Takes So Long
snippet.description:
A phone charges fast at first and slows near full on purpose: when the graphite in its battery is almost full, a strong current can leave lithium as metal on the surface, so the charger holds the voltage and lets the current fade.

New Shorts every day.

SOURCES
- Two-stage charging (constant current, then constant voltage), the 70 percent fast stage and why saturation adds stress: https://batteryuniversity.com/article/bu-409-charging-lithium-ion
- Lithium plating on graphite anodes during fast charging causes capacity loss and safety risks: https://deepblue.lib.umich.edu/items/e193b4c5-58e5-4706-b6be-8e4dc0e1468a
- Fully lithiated graphite sits close to the potential of metallic lithium: https://ossila.com/pages/lithium-plating
- iPhone Optimized Battery Charging pauses at 80 percent and finishes before you usually unplug: https://support.apple.com/en-us/108055
Where the slow stage starts differs by phone and by battery. Only the Battery University page was read in full; the other sources were checked from search summaries. Cut-off 9 October 2026. Figures checked on 9 October 2026.

snippet.title: Deep-Sea Mining: The Rulebook Is Still Unfinished

snippet.title: Most Computer Chips Start in Rock From One Small Town
snippet.description:
Most computer chips start in a quartz crucible, and most of that quartz comes from one small town in North Carolina: Spruce Pine. Why a silicon crystal needs ultra-pure quartz, and what stopped after Hurricane Helene in 2024.

New Shorts every day.

SOURCES
- Wikipedia, Spruce Pine Mining District (about 70 to 90 % of the world's high-purity quartz; molten silicon reacts with almost all materials except quartz above 1,400 C; Helene 2024; stockpiled crucibles prevented immediate shortages): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spruce_Pine_Mining_District
- The Quartz Corp, Silicon wafer production (one crucible pulls about 8 ingots in about 400 hours; a 300 mm ingot yields about 2 million chips): https://www.thequartzcorp.com/silicon-wafer-production
- The Quartz Corp, Geology (pegmatites almost free from inclusions): https://www.thequartzcorp.com/geology
- Sibelco, High-purity quartz (two uniquely pure ore bodies at Spruce Pine; crucibles for the Czochralski process): https://www.sibelco.com/materials/high-purity-quartz
The 16 million chips per crucible is a rough calculation from the Quartz Corp figures above (chip sizes vary). The share of supply differs by source (about 70 to 90 %). Figures checked on 5 October 2026.

PHOTO CREDITS (Wikimedia Commons)
Downtown Spruce Pine, used crucible photos, silicon boule and 1956 crystal puller: public domain | Silicon wafer: Peellden, CC BY-SA 3.0 | Silicon crystal: Massimiliano Lincetto, CC BY-SA 4.0 | Pegmatite rock (Ruggles mine, New Hampshire, shown as an example of the rock type): James St. John, CC BY 2.0 | Hurricane Helene damage (Buncombe County, North Carolina): NCDOT Communications, CC BY 2.0

snippet.title: The First Metal-Type Book Is Not the Gutenberg Bible
snippet.description:
The first book printed with metal type is not the Gutenberg Bible. It is the Jikji, a Korean book from 1377, and its printer's mistakes are the proof.

New Shorts every day.

SOURCES
- BnF (Bibliotheque nationale de France), Jikji, treasure of the world of printing (printed 1377 at Heungdeok Temple, Cheongju; provenance; free on Gallica): https://bnf.fr/en/jikji-treasure-world-printing
- Global Jikji, Movable Metal Type of Goryeo Korea (the postscript: "printed with cast metal type at Heungdeoksa Temple outside Cheongju Magistracy"): https://www.globaljikji.org/en/sub.do?menukey=4103
- Open Culture, The oldest book printed with movable type is not the Gutenberg Bible (September 2026): https://www.openculture.com/2026/09/the-oldest-book-printed-with-movable-type-is-not-the-gutenberg-bible-jikji.html
- Wikipedia, Jikji (the upside-down, omitted and tilted characters scholars cite as evidence of loose metal type): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jikji
- From Jikji to Gutenberg, University of Utah: https://jikji.utah.edu/
The Gutenberg Bible is dated 1450 to 1455 depending on the source, so the gap is 73 to 78 years. Figures checked on 5 October 2026.

snippet.title: EV Battery Life: Only 2% a Year, and Charging Matters Most
snippet.description:
Electric car batteries lose about 2% of their capacity a year. What wears them faster (fast charging, heat), what cold really costs (range, mostly the heater), and why packs got cheaper (iron phosphate chemistry).

New Shorts every day.

SOURCES
- Geotab, EV Battery Health Study, 13 January 2026 (2.3% a year across 22,700+ vehicles; fast charging above 100 kW up to 3.0% a year against about 1.5%; hot regions about 0.4% a year more): https://www.geotab.com/press-release/ev-battery-health-degradation-fast-charging-study/
- BloombergNEF, Battery Price Survey, December 2025 ($108 per kWh average pack, down 8%; LFP $81 against NMC $128): https://about.bnef.com/insights/clean-transport/lithium-ion-battery-pack-prices-fall-to-108-per-kilowatt-hour-despite-rising-metal-prices-bloombergnef/
- AAA cold-weather range tests, May 2026 (39% less range at 20 F with climate control; as reported by Autoblog): https://www.autoblog.com/news/aaa-finds-ev-range-drops-39-in-cold-weather-and-costs-jump
- Wang et al., Fast charging of lithium-ion batteries at all temperatures, PNAS 2018 (lithium plating in the cold, SEI growth in the heat): https://ecec.me.psu.edu/Pubs/2018_June_PNAS.pdf
Figures checked on 5 October 2026. The 2.3% is an average, not a guarantee; the claim that most of the cold-weather loss is the cabin heater is the reading of AAA's tests in press summaries.
